newsitem.title: UK: EMERGING MARKET OUTLOOK - Peru crisis, Bulgaria lead.
newsitem.headline: EMERGING MARKET OUTLOOK - Peru crisis, Bulgaria lead.

text.p: Latin America will keep emerging market investors well focused over the Christmas week as a hostage crisis wears on in Peru and Chile posts its monthly GDP series, analysts say.
But they will also be following developments in BULGARIA following the surprise resignation of prime minister Zhan Videnov on Saturday, leaving the crisis-hit country without an effective government.

But most Latam watchers are still stunned by events in PERU, where a gang of left-wing guerrillas have been holding a glittering array of diplomats, ministers and business officials hostage since Tuesday in the most violent incident Peru has seen for several years.
Late on Sunday the rebels freed 225 of the hostages but kept about 140 captive as a bargaining tool.
"This terrorist incident is likely to shake investor and consumer confidence, and could possibly threaten the expected recovery in Peru next year," Foreign & Colonial Emerging Markets said.
Last week's sell-off of Peruvian assets on the perception of increased risk may provoke some bargain hunting this week, some investors say.

"There may be a bit of buying even if the crisis is unresolved as players recognise the market has overshot and see there is scope for buying," said James Montier, Latin America economist at Kleinwort Benson Securities.
He said President Alberto Fujimori was unlikely to emerge from the crisis unscathed, looking bad if he gives in to the guerrillas' demands but seeing no easy solutions at hand if he doesn't.
The IFC's Peru index shed nearly 3.5 points over the week to Friday as the stand-off wore on.
Economic data in CHILE and MEXICO will otherwise keep Latin America investors on their toes.
"Economic activity in CHILE will be closely watched when it publishes its monthly (October) GDP series on Monday," Montier, said.

"It is likely to show a bit of a bounce -- we've seen a slowing down to about five percent in September and October is expected to be around seven percent, but this is mostly due to a working days problem," he added.
A boost to the October year-on-year figure will not signal an economic acceleration, he said, since October 1996 had two more working days than the same month the previous year.
But he said consumer sector stocks might bounce on the news.
Kleinwort Benson is forecasting 1996 GDP growth of around 6.6 percent, slowing to around 5.0 or 5.5 percent in 1997, and investors will be looking for a rate cut in the first quarter.
MEXICO's trade balance data for November is expected to emerge during the week, with the market looking for a surplus just under $500 million.
Of more concern in some quarters is the Mexican peso, which some analysts reckon is still overvalued.

"Even if we don't get (our 8.5 percent year-end target) this side of Christmas it should be 10 percent lower," said Kleinwort Benson's Montier. "It's a relatively significant amount and it's showing up in the trade data," he added.
East European investors meanwhile will be digesting the outcome of a tumulous weekend in BULGARIA.
Bulgarian debt prices shed up to a full point early on Monday as a show-down between hardliners and reformists entered its final phase, with Congress preparing to vote for a new prime minister.

The political battle looks set to further delay much needed economic reform. A team of IMF experts left Sofia on Friday after helping the government prepare legal measures for setting up a currency board to steady the crisis-hit lev.

In RUSSIA, President Boris Yeltsin returns to work this week after parliament approved the second reading of the 1997 draft budget late on Friday. Analysts say it may go back to the Duma for its third reading on Christmas Day or possibly Friday.

"It would be best if they got it done before the end of the calendar year and the Duma is scheduled to meet on Christmas Day," said David Mars, director of emerging markets European economic research at SBC Warburg.
Investors in POLAND meanwhile will be keeping an eye out for a possible interest rate rise of one to two percent, which may take place during the quieter Christmas period.
Such a rise would boost the zloty but would be negative for T-bills and its equity markets, especially exporters, Mars said.
Elsewhere, INDIA faces a Monday deadline for electing a successor to P.V. Narasimha Rao, who resigned last week as Congress party president.
ISRAEL debates its 1997 budget on Monday and CUBA will hold a working session on its 1997 budget on Christmas eve.
The IFC emerging market composite investable index, IFC/IPRD, denominated in dollars, was up 1.8 percent at 291.03 points after Friday's close, compared with a week ago.
Latin America was up 3.1 percent week-on-week at 529.59, Asia was up 0.4 at 249.60, and Europe, Middle East and Africa was up 2.8 at 132.65. --London Newsroom +44 171 542 2734
